summary: SkyShift is a public-facing sky exploration web tool designed to make changes in the infrared universe easier to see. Users enter Right Ascension and declination or select an example target, choose a field of view and detector array and explore multiple observations of the same sky region over time. A blink player highlights apparent motion while a difference view and mean stack help users compare images. The project includes a connection to NASA/IPAC's public SPHEREx archive, designed to retrieve DR1 and QR3 spectral-image cutouts and align their sky coordinates for comparison. An explicitly labelled simulation mode makes the interface accessible even when live data is unavailable. SkyShift aims to give students, citizen scientists and curious people a more approachable starting point for investigating moving or changing objects. It presents candidate changes for further investigation rather than claiming new discoveries or replacing scientific validation.
details:
What did you develop?

We developed SkyShift, an interactive browser-based interface for exploring the same patch of sky across multiple observations. Its main features are editable Right Ascension and declination, five named target presets, adjustable field of view, selectable SPHEREx detector arrays, a time slider, animated blink playback, mean stacking, image subtraction, metadata tables and shareable URLs. Users can explore a built-in educational simulation or request public SPHEREx archive observations in live mode.

How does it work?

In live mode, a Python HTTP backend searches NASA/IPAC IRSA's IVOA Simple Image Access v2 service for DR1 and QR3 spectral-image exposures that cover the selected position. It selects observations for the requested detector, retrieves small multi-extension FITS cutouts through IRSA's cutout service, reads the calibrated IMAGE data, masks pixels where the FLAGS bitmask is nonzero and reprojects the observations to a common north-up World Coordinate System grid. The browser visualizes the image data using HTML Canvas. Users can play observations over time, compare two epochs through subtraction or make an average stack. The display retains the same brightness scale across frames. Each real frame includes the observation identifier, timestamp and link back to the source FITS file.

The simulation mode creates a deliberately exaggerated moving point and brightness-variable point against a synthetic star field. The interface visibly labels the simulation as non-NASA data.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

SkyShift lowers the technical barrier to time-domain exploration by making astronomic images easier to navigate and compare. It supports science education, introductory citizen-science discovery work and early investigation of candidate moving or variable sources. Researchers and experienced volunteers can then follow up using archived original data and accepted scientific methods. No automatic asteroid, planet or brown-dwarf discovery is asserted.

What technologies did you use?

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, Canvas 2D.
  • Backend: Python 3.10+ standard-library HTTP server and IRSA requests through urllib.
  • Live scientific processing: NumPy, Astropy (FITS, WCS, time), SciPy (pixel resampling).
  • Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA public SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 Spectral Image MEFs, when live mode successfully connects.
  • Distribution: open-source code repository and optional hosted Python web service.

How is it creative?

The interface combines familiar citizen-science-style blink comparison with transparent scientific data provenance. It keeps simulation and real imagery separate and makes the observation sequence, array selection, field width and difference product accessible with a simple workflow. Deep-link URL parameters allow others to share a specific sky region. The lightweight Python server enables a self-contained educational experience without a large application framework.

What factors did you consider?

We considered public accessibility, image-registration consistency, robust input validation, open datasets, reference provenance, server-side access to FITS images, performance, remote service failures, masking of flagged data and honest distinction between a demonstration and verified astronomical analysis. Different SPHEREx exposures may cover different effective infrared wavelengths, so apparent brightness changes are not automatically evidence of intrinsic variability or physical motion. The tool supports exploration, not calibrated scientific conclusions.

Limitations and next features

The live mode needs real archive access and its network path has not been end-to-end tested in the provided build environment. The interface does not yet visualize all 102 spectral channels independently, produce spectra, identify moving sources automatically, integrate Gaia/WISE overlays or establish scientific significance. Those are future features rather than features to claim already developed. The user must review live results and verify coverage, flags, epochs and spectral comparability.
